prompt: In living organisms, what is the substrate for a nucleophilic acyl substitution reaction generally?

choices.text: A thioester or an acyl phosphate
An acid chloride or an acid anhydride
choices.why: These react so rapidly with water that they can't exist for long in living organisms.

choices.text: An amide
choices.why: Amides are the least reactive derivatives and are stable in water. They aren't the usual acyl donors.

choices.text: A free carboxylic acid
choices.why: Carboxylic acids don't undergo direct acyl substitution in biological chemistry. They must be activated first.

explanation: The substrate for nucleophilic acyl substitution in living organisms is generally either a thioester (RCOSR′) or an acyl phosphate (RCO2PO3^2− or RCO2PO3R′^−).

prompt: Why are thioesters and acyl phosphates suited to be the acyl donors in living organisms?

choices.text: They are stable enough to exist in cells yet reactive enough for acyl substitution
They are more reactive than acid chlorides, so they react fastest
choices.why: Neither is as reactive as an acid chloride or acid anhydride.

choices.text: They are completely unreactive toward nucleophiles in cells
choices.why: They do react: acyl CoAs, for example, transfer their acyl groups to amines.

choices.text: They are the least reactive of all the carboxylic acid derivatives
choices.why: Amides are the least reactive. Thioesters and acyl phosphates are more reactive than esters.

explanation: Neither a thioester nor an acyl phosphate is as reactive as an acid chloride or acid anhydride, yet both are stable enough to exist in living organisms while still reactive enough to undergo acyl substitution.

prompt: What are the most common thioesters in nature?

choices.text: Acyl CoAs, such as acetyl CoA
Acyl adenylates, such as acetyl adenylate
choices.why: Acyl adenylates are mixed anhydrides of a carboxylic acid and AMP, not thioesters.

choices.text: Lactones, such as butyrolactone
choices.why: Lactones are cyclic esters, with oxygen rather than sulfur.

choices.text: Acyl phosphates, such as benzoyl phosphate
choices.why: Acyl phosphates, RCO2PO3^2−, are a separate class of biological acid derivative.

explanation: Acyl CoAs, such as acetyl CoA, are the most common thioesters in nature. They form when coenzyme A reacts with an acyl phosphate or acyl adenylate.

prompt: Coenzyme A is a thiol in which phosphopantetheine and adenosine 3′,5′-bisphosphate are joined. What kind of linkage joins them?

choices.text: A phosphoric anhydride linkage
A thioester linkage, –CO–S–
choices.why: The thioester forms only when CoA is acylated. The link inside CoA is a phosphoric anhydride.

choices.text: An amide linkage, –CO–NH–
choices.why: The two parts are joined through phosphorus, by an O=P–O–P=O link.

choices.text: A carbon–carbon bond
choices.why: The two parts are joined through a phosphoric anhydride link, not a C–C bond.

explanation: Coenzyme A is a thiol formed by a phosphoric anhydride linkage (O=P–O–P=O) between phosphopantetheine and adenosine 3′,5′-bisphosphate.

prompt: How many phosphate groups does adenosine 3′,5′-bisphosphate have?
explanation: The prefix bis- means "two": adenosine 3′,5′-bisphosphate has two phosphate groups, one on carbon 3′ and one on carbon 5′.

prompt: When coenzyme A reacts with acetyl adenylate to give acetyl CoA, which group of coenzyme A is the nucleophile?

choices.text: The thiol (–SH) group
A phosphate oxygen
choices.why: The product, acetyl CoA, is a thioester, so the acetyl group must bond to sulfur.

choices.text: A hydroxyl (–OH) group
choices.why: Bonding through oxygen would give an ester, but acetyl CoA is a thioester.

choices.text: An amide nitrogen
choices.why: Bonding through nitrogen would give an amide, but acetyl CoA is a thioester with a C–S bond.

explanation: Coenzyme A is a thiol. Its –SH group carries out a nucleophilic acyl substitution on acetyl adenylate to give the thioester acetyl CoA (Figure 21.8.1).

prompt: In the formation of acetyl CoA from coenzyme A and acetyl adenylate, what leaving group is expelled?

choices.text: Adenosine monophosphate (AMP)
Diphosphate ion released from ATP
choices.why: Diphosphate leaves in the earlier step, when the carboxylate reacts with ATP to make the acyl adenylate.

choices.text: The thiolate of coenzyme A
choices.why: Coenzyme A is the nucleophile. Its sulfur stays bonded to the acetyl group in acetyl CoA.

choices.text: Hydroxide ion from water
choices.why: The acetyl group is bonded to AMP in acetyl adenylate, and AMP is what leaves.

explanation: Acetyl adenylate is a mixed anhydride of acetic acid and AMP. When the –SH of coenzyme A attacks the acyl carbon, AMP is expelled and acetyl CoA forms (Figures 21.3.3 and 21.8.1).

prompt: N-Acetylglucosamine, a component of cartilage, is made from glucosamine and acetyl CoA. What kind of reaction is this?

choices.text: Aminolysis: the amine of glucosamine replaces the –SCoA group, forming an amide
Hydrolysis: water replaces the –SCoA group, forming acetic acid
choices.why: The product is an amide, N-acetylglucosamine, so the nucleophile is the amine of glucosamine, not water.

choices.text: Alcoholysis: an –OH of glucosamine forms an acetate ester
choices.why: The N- in N-acetylglucosamine shows the acetyl group is on nitrogen, so an amide forms, not an ester.

choices.text: Reduction: hydride from NADPH converts acetyl CoA into an aldehyde
choices.why: No reducing agent is involved. The acetyl group is transferred to the amine.

explanation: N-Acetylglucosamine is synthesized by an aminolysis reaction between glucosamine and acetyl CoA. The amine nitrogen replaces the –SCoA group, giving an amide and HSCoA.

prompt: In the biosynthesis of mevaldehyde, (3S)-3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl CoA is reduced by hydride from NADPH. What happens to its thioester group?

choices.text: It is partially reduced to an aldehyde
It is reduced all the way to a primary alcohol
choices.why: This is a partial reduction: hydride substitutes for –SCoA, and the product is an aldehyde, mevaldehyde.

choices.text: It is converted into an amide
choices.why: Making an amide would need an amine nucleophile. Here the nucleophile is hydride.

choices.text: It is hydrolyzed to a carboxylic acid
choices.why: Hydrolysis would need water as the nucleophile. NADPH donates hydride.

explanation: In this nucleophilic acyl substitution on a thioester, hydride ion from NADPH replaces the –SCoA group, effecting a partial reduction of the thioester to an aldehyde in the biosynthesis of mevaldehyde.

prompt: Formation of an acyl adenylate from a carboxylic acid and ATP is a nucleophilic acyl substitution that takes place at which atom?

choices.text: Phosphorus
The carbonyl carbon of the acid
choices.why: In this step the carboxylate is the nucleophile. It adds to a P=O bond of ATP.

choices.text: Sulfur
choices.why: Sulfur is involved later, when the –SH of coenzyme A attacks the acyl adenylate.

choices.text: Nitrogen
choices.why: The substitution in this step happens at a phosphorus atom of ATP.

explanation: Formation of the acyl adenylate occurs by reaction of a carboxylic acid with ATP and is itself a nucleophilic acyl substitution that takes place on phosphorus (Section 21.3).
